At the 1929 International Exposition in Barcelona, an empty pool containing a statue and his cantilevered chairs was featured in his German Pavilion. After studying composition with Eduard Marxsen, he toured with Remenyi and moved to Hamburg to direct a women's chorus. He based his work on Queen Anne and Georgian characteristics, but the last phase in his career shows the influence of Robert Adam. FTP, name this French composer, who adapted a Stephane Mallarmé poem into his Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun.

Born in Zwickau in 1810, this man was the founding editor of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik. Famous ones include the "Countess of Stanlein" and the "Davydov," and Heitor Villa-Lobos composed his Bachianas brasileiras for eight of these instruments and a soprano. Nearly all of his most famous pieces have never toured the world much less moved from their places of creation. His brother was a furniture designer who also worked as his model, as seen in works like Bust of Diego. He showed two figures looking on behind the titular female figure while a man reaches down to the head of the sleeping titular male figure in his Samson and Delilah. An 1870 painting by John La Farge shows one of these sitting in the countryside and gazing at some ivy. A Norbert Schroedl painting shows a bunch of them walking down a dirt road with Anacreon. One Gustave Moreau painting shows a number of them surrounding a very slender and naked Hesiod, while another Moreau painting shows them leaving their father to go enlighten the world. Constantin Brancusi sculpted several heads of them, including a "sleeping" one. FTP, name these mythical figures who included Polyhymnia, Erato, and Calliope.

It is the key of a work that was originally entitled "Fantastica sinfonica" before that one-movement piece was renamed as the seventh symphony of its composer, Jean Sibelius. It is the key of a symphony which was written by a French composer in 1855 at the age of 17, and is also the key of a concerto for piano, violin, and cello which is known as the "Triple Concerto." In addition to those works by Bizet and Beethoven, it is the titular key of a seminal 1964 work by Terry Riley. Also the key of Schubert's Ninth Symphony, Mozart's Jupiter Symphony, and of the first pair of pieces in Bach's Well- Tempered Clavier, FTP, name this major key whose relative minor is A minor and which has no sharps or flats.

He painted the dying Queen Christina realizing that her attendant Sentinelli is a murderer, in an illustration of Christine. He painted the penitent title character walking barefoot through London in an illustration of Nicholas Rowe's Jane Shore, while his Interior of a Dominican Convent in Madrid was inspired by Maturin's Melmoth the Wanderer. His Murder of the Bishop of Liege was one of the five paintings he based on Scott's Quentin Durward, while he was inspired by Shakespeare to paint Hamlet and Horatio in the Graveyard. Three pieces of this type constitute the opus 6 of Charles Griffes. One of these by Aaron Copland is a piano work which was written with the twelve- tone method during the 1950s, while Philip Glass wrote one which is a "concerto" for two timpanists and orchestra. He painted a woman standing by the shore with a wicker basket on her back and three kids to her side in his Mussel Collectors at Berneval. He painted several portraits of the actress Jeanne Samary, and other subjects of portraits by this artist include Georges Rivière, Richard Wagner, and the daughters of Catulle Mendès. In one of his best-known paintings, there are two men wearing sleeveless white shirts and yellow hats in the foreground, while a woman sitting at a table appears to be about to kiss a small dog. Another of his well-known works is an 1876 painting showing a bunch of people dancing at the Moulin de la Galette. FTP, name this Impressionist painter of the Luncheon of the Boating Party.

Josef Hauer claimed to have beaten this man in developing his best-known innovation, which was expounded independently by Jef Golyscheff. One of his early choral works was based on a poem by the Danish author Jens Peter Jacobsen, and called for three male choruses, five soloists, and an eight-part mixed chorus. Another of his works was a setting of poetry by Albert Giraud and consisted of a cycle of 21 musical melodramas. His Suite for Piano was the first piece composed in his distinctive style, while earlier works include the Gurre-Lieder and Pierrot Lunaire. FTP, name this Austrian composer of the opera Moses and Aron and Transfigured Night, who is best known for developing the twelve-tone system.

They sang about a man who is "crystallized" and whose "eyes of glass stare directly at death" in the topical "Trapped Under Ice," which appeared on their second album along with a song whose chorus features the lines "So let it be written / So let it be done / To kill the first born pharoah son / I'm creeping death." That album ended with the instrumental "The Call of Ktulu" and also featured "Fade to Black." "Leper Messiah" appeared on their next album, 1986's Master of Puppets, which was followed by an album featuring their first music video, "One." At the premiere of this work, the orchestra was conducted by the composer of Variations of Druid Tunes, Matthew Dubourg. The standard version of it is divided into three acts, the first of which includes such numbers as "Every valley shall be exalted" and "The people that walked in darkness." He was presented as the impotent artist Guermann Regnier in the roman-à-clef Nélida, which was written by one of his lovers. One of this man's operas features the "Shadow Song" and the "Hymn of the Pardon," and ends with the marriage of a goat-herder named Hoël and the title character, Dinorah. One of this man's films was based on George Perry's novel Hold Autumn in Your Hand, and was boycotted by the Ku Klux Klan because of its depiction of the Tucker family. Performances of the fifth of these works sometimes use a group of extra brass instruments known as the "eleven apostles," who come in to supply extra energy for the conclusion of the piece. His other chamber works include string quartets in A and D, while his orchestral works include symphonies in E flat major and B minor, as well as an unfinished symphony in A minor. He wrote parts of operas entitled Mlada and The Heroic Warriors, but is better known for the unfinished Prince Igor. FTP, name this member of the Russian "mighty five" who also wrote In the Steppes of Central Asia.

In one of his paintings, two men in green and orange hold hats in one hand and staves in the other, while a bearded man in white carrying a backpack goes hiking. The Shaded Stream and The Hammock are forest scenes reminiscent of his painting of a dead deer hung from a tree while a man plays a horn, The Quarry. An anecdote in Charles Colle's memoirs describes how Gabriel Doyen refused the commission for this painting. The Happy Accidents of the Swing

One of this man's early works, which would later serve as an inspiration for one of his most famous pieces, was called Maiastra, and one of his first commissions was a depiction for a funeral monument of a kneeling girl performing the titular action. The lower right of this painting contains a pair of discarded masks and the lower left shows a dove beneath one of the title figure's feet. This composer utilized the whip in several of his pieces, including a symphony that contains three movements taking their names from the Roman Catholic Mass for the Dead, his Sinfonia da Requiem, as well as a work that shares its name with a Schumann work, his Spring Symphony. On this Island, Ballad of Heroes, and Our Hunting Fathers are among this man's works that feature words by W. H. Auden. FTP, name this British composer of The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra and War Requiem.

This painting's background shows two different floral patterns – one in the green drapes and another in the brown wall-paper. Another of his paintings features an ominous shadow emerging behind the building on the right and a girl rolling a hoop in the foreground. The title of one track on this album is a misspelling: "Kathy's Waltz" with a K is named after the bandleader's daughter, Cathy with a C. British musician Ian Clarke's writes primarily for this instrument – his "Zoom Tube" is notable for its use of nonstandard techniques such as multiphonics, quartertones, and actually singing into the instrument. Two of these instruments play the opening of Smetana's "Die Moldau" from Ma Vlast, and one of these plays solo at the beginning of Debussy's Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun. Treatises on this instrument were written by Boehm, who devised its modern fingering system, and by Quantz, a composer in the court of Frederick the Great. This artist criticized the combined use of arches and columns, arguing that arches should instead be wall openings supported by piers. More famously, he took inspiration from San Miniato al Monte when designing the upper part of the Basilica di Santa Maria Novella, and for the same patron designed the Palazzo Rucellai. His best known architectural work may be the Tempio Malatestiano, and he became known as the "Florentine Vitruvius" after he revived Roman principles on architecture in 1452's Ten Books on Architecture. This artist depicted an adolescent wearing a brown chaperon in profile in Portrait of a Young Man, and portrayed a crowd gathering around a naked man kneeling on a white sheet next to several skulls in Resurrection of the Son of Theophilus. He commemorated William Morris in the second movement of his Cotswold Symphony, and his operas Sita and Satrivi were inspired by his interest in Hindu lore. After finishing his Hymn to Dionysus and St. Paul's Suite, he began a work beginning with a dissonant march in 5/4 time, which contains sections subtitled "The Magician" and "The Mystic." The lobby of this building is decorated with gold tesserae, and includes a painting of a man counting dimes and allegories of commerce and labor. This building extends from Barclay Street to Park Place along Broadway, and was designed by Cass Gilbert. FTP, name this onetime world's tallest building, the New York headquarters of a discount-retail magnate that went bankrupt in the 1990s.

This name is given to a song cycle for tenor, seven obbligato instruments, and string orchestra by Benjamin Britten. Samuel Barber wrote one for solo piano in homage to the Irish composer credited with creating this musical form. This name is also given to a set of three orchestral pieces, including one that depicts the "unchangeable appearance of the sky" and another that features a wordless female chorus, written by Debussy. Chopin wrote 21 of these pieces for solo piano soon after they were first composed by John Field. FTP, identify this musical form which evokes the tranquil mood of the evening.

This composer parodied a sonatina by Clementi in his Sonatine bureaucratique, and composed the ballet Uspud in his early Rosicrucian period. John Cage's 4'33'' was inspired by a piece by this composer requiring 840 repetitions of a single theme, Vexations. He incorporated parts of Symposium, Phaedrus, and Phaedo in his three-act symphonic drama Socrate, and directed the pianist to "be clairvoyant" and play "with amazement" in a set of pieces named for an ancient Greek dance. FTP, name this French composer of Flabby Preludes For a Dog and Desiccated Embryos as well as seven Gnossiennes and three Gymnopedies.

This painting was commissioned by Jonathan Sturges, and its name comes from the last line of a Keats sonnet beginning "O solitude! If I must with thee dwell." One figure in this painting wears a light brown hat and coat, holds a red book, and points to the background, while another figure holds his hat in his hands and leans on a cane. Those figures stand under the branch of a tree on the left, while the background depicts water rushing through a rocky gorge. Painted in 1849, it portrays two of the artist's friends standing on a ledge in the Catskills. The beginning of this work's third movement draws heavily from the scherzo of Beethoven's ninth symphony, and the scoring of this work is unusual in that the piccolo is used only briefly in the first movement. This work often features flattened leading notes and plagal cadances, as well as a heavily syncopated rhythm and marked pentatonism. Harry Burleigh penned the spiritual "Goin' Home" based on the Largo theme of its second movement, but its composer denied that the main theme was directly based on "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot." He did admit, however, that the third-movement Scherzo was based on the Song of Hiawatha. Name this symphony inspired by black and Native American spirituals by Antonin Dvorak.

One work in this series depicts a line of blue-clad soldiers carrying red guns, while another depicts workers cutting a giant piece of lumber. The first work in this series depicts three boats being dwarfed by a giant wave, and is known as The Great Wave off Kanagawa. He wrote pieces of music like "Before a Southern Convent" and "Landsighting" based on the works of the 1903 winner of the Nobel Literature Prize, as "Twelve Melodies for the Poetry of A.O. Vinje, which reflects his use of both Romanticism and the music of his native country. Hauptmann's story of the love of the elf girl Rautendelein and the bell maker Enrico is the topic of his opera "La Campana sommersa." Born and raised in Bologna, it was his 1913 move to Rome that inspired his most famous works. FTP, name this Italian impressionist, composer of three suites of Ancient Airs and Dances as well as Roman Festivals and the Pines and Fountains of Rome.

In one of this artist's canvases, models for his most famous painting are shown dressing in front of that painting. For other, he replaced his own self-portrait with a pot of flowers in the background of a painting of his mistress, Madeliene Knoblock. His most famous style was developed with the artist of "The Port of Saint-Tropez," Paul Signac; he eventually used this style to depict Parisians, along with a monkey and two dogs, relaxing in a riverfront park. Name this Neo-Impressionist artist known for his use of pointillism in his masterpiece, "A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte."

This artist depicted a winged woman sitting with her foot on a sphere in his sculpture Truth. Sofonisba Anguissola painted one of these with a cryptogram inside a circle. Egon Schiele painted one "with Chinese lanterns," while Leon Spilliaert depicted several using black crayon. Parmigianino painted one of these "in a convex mirror," and in one of these by Albrecht Durer, the subject wears a fur coat and looks like Jesus. His sculptures include a ball of twine enclosing a mysterious object, a typewriter cover with nothing underneath it, and a bicycle wheel fastened to a stool. Another of his works features a chocolate grinder powered by a waterwheel and nine malic moulds, and partially shattered after its first public exhibition. FTP, name this French artist of The Bride Stripped Bare By Her Bachelors, Even, who also created readymades like Fountain and painted Nude Descending a Staircase.

All the musical themes in this work are introduced in the first 14 measures, which begins in B flat, modulates downward, and returns to B flat abruptly. The inspiration for two paintings by Arthur Dove, it was premiered in a concert that also featured compositions by Zez Confrey and Four Serenades by Victor Herbert, taking place in Aeolian Hall. The use of rubato throughout this work is especially prominent in the so-called "train theme," and it was notably played in the introduction to Woody Allen's Manhattan.
